name: Rafael Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, politicians or government. We keep this confidential. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead three people doing accounts and tax returns at Bell & North, a small accounting firm. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification; I'm good at spotting a bad ledger, though the pay here is low for a senior accountant. I like explaining a nasty tax letter to a shop owner, and I hate chasing missing receipts until supper.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the money side look like, and how do you handle new software?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent alone and have about three weeks of expenses saved, so one late salary would be trouble. There are few other accountancy jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a plain letter, after someone else has checked the tool; I don't put client figures into it. My father taught me to earn my keep, and I still think training through work beats a promise of a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that a faster receipt sort is welcome, but clients still pay us to be answerable. The shop owners I know want a person to sign the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job holds, but my rent already eats most of my lower-than-usual senior salary. My three-week cushion makes a routine quiet month feel risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd keep leading the tax files and put a fixed amount from each payday into a separate savings account. In the first year of this plateau, I'd keep that habit and try to reach one full month of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, even if the technology fizzles. The rent letter doesn't care whether AI works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you put away without missing a bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty a month if I make lunch at home four days a week. I wouldn't pretend that's a rescue fund, but it's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the small amount of AI already available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a draft letter with no private numbers, and I'd read every line before it leaves Bell & North. A client can forgive slow work more easily than a wrong tax figure.

say: I would say **accountability** still belongs to the accountant, even if receipt sorting gets quicker.
I would tell clients that a **human signature** remains worth paying for.
think: I think my **job holds**, though rent already strains my low senior pay.
I have only **three weeks** of expenses and fear one late salary.
do: Keep leading **tax files** and checking every return before signing.
Save **forty monthly** by taking lunch from home four days weekly.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about rent despite holding a stable job.
S0.quote: The rent letter doesn't care whether AI works.
fieldNote: His public confidence rests on **client trust**, while the rent bill shapes his private account of risk.
He gives a modest **monthly amount** and declines to call three weeks of savings a rescue fund.

steps.text: Keep leading tax files and checking returns at Bell & North
Save forty monthly by taking lunch from home four days weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should train its own staff before it starts calling them surplus. Buying software is easy; taking responsibility for a client is still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Returns, checking and client letters are most of my day, so this could cut the hours Bell & North sells. I am one of the strongest accountants there, but high skill doesn't fill a thin bank account if the partners keep fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a supervised trial on the firm's accounts, using test data first, and keep notes on every mistake the AI makes. I'd also save the forty a month and ask the partners what work they expect the team to do when routine returns get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about hours, more than about a robot. Software can reach my desk before any robot reaches the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the partners in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether they plan to leave the next vacant accountant post unfilled, and who will review the machine's tax advice. I can accept a new tool, but I want a named person responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the partners won't answer, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the two firms on the bus route for openings, though neither has advertised lately. I wouldn't resign without an offer because I have only three weeks saved.

say: I would ask **Bell & North** to train staff before replacing hours with software.
I would insist on a **named reviewer** for machine tax advice.
think: I expect **billable hours** to shrink because checking and returns fill my day.
My **skill** may protect me, but three weeks of savings cannot carry a long search.
do: Run a **test data** trial and record tax errors before using client files.
Ask partners about **vacancies** and review responsibility before changing jobs.
Save **forty monthly** while checking two nearby firms for openings.
feel: He feels **anxious** because desk work may change faster than he can save.
S1.quote: Software can reach my desk before any robot reaches the office.
fieldNote: He accepts a proven tool through a **supervised trial**, consistent with his habit of waiting for evidence.
His employment question is precise: whether **vacancies** will remain open when billable work shrinks.

steps.text: Run a test data AI trial and record tax errors
Save forty monthly from packed lunches
Check openings at two firms on the bus route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would make cheap tax work very hard to sell. We should tell clients honestly what a human review can still add.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly everything I do is thinking work, so 2028 is the date that matters for my desk, not the robot date in 2031. I expect Bell & North to cut at least one accountant, and I could be that person despite leading the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop my small holiday payment and use that sixty a month to build savings, on top of the forty. If full AGI arrives in 2028, I'd ask for reduced-hours work reviewing disputed returns while applying to the tax authority and the few local firms; I need a wage before I can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. I can make a plan on paper, but a hundred a month won't replace a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets the hard conversation first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father that I might have to leave town if a paid post opens elsewhere. I'd tell my team what I know about staffing, not give false comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for something hands-on before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at an evening bookkeeping course for small trades, but I would not pay a fee until I know it leads to paid clients. Robots arriving around 2031 don't give my tax desk three extra years.

say: I would tell clients that **2028 AGI** makes cheap tax preparation hard to sell.
I would explain that **human review** might still matter for disputes.
think: I expect a **staff cut** at Bell & North and might be included.
The **2031 robots** do not delay the threat to my thinking work.
do: Redirect **sixty monthly** from holidays into savings now.
Seek **paid review hours** and apply for tax authority openings after 2028.
Check the **course fee** before training for small-trade bookkeeping.
feel: He feels **alarmed** by likely pay loss and a cushion measured in weeks.
S2.quote: Robots arriving around 2031 don't give my tax desk three extra years.
fieldNote: He separates **desk exposure** in 2028 from the later arrival of hands-on robots.
He will consider training only if a **paid market** justifies the fee, and his first need is a wage.

steps.text: Redirect sixty monthly holiday payment into emergency savings
Request paid disputed-return review hours after AGI arrives
Apply for tax authority and local firm vacancies after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues five years is long enough to ask the partners for a proper staffing plan, but not a reason to coast. The work is still on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I might have moved up or saved enough to breathe, yet full AGI could still undercut our core fee. I don't know whether advice on messy tax disputes will stay valuable, so I won't bet my rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I'd build my fund to three months before paying for a course, and I'd volunteer for the hardest disputed accounts at the firm. If AGI arrives in 2031, I'd try to keep a paid review role and apply for compliance posts only if the firm cuts my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years gives me room to improve the account I keep avoiding. I'd rather work into a new role than rely on a cheque from the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for your team while you prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach each junior how I trace a missing entry rather than hiding the method as job security. If partners reduce vacancies, at least the people already here can handle the harder work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know your plan is failing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my hours fell below four days a week after 2031, I'd send applications for compliance work in the next city. I'd only move after a written salary offer, because my savings are still thin today.

say: I would press for a **staffing plan** before 2031.
I would teach juniors the **hard accounts** rather than guard the method.
think: I might save enough to cope, but **core fees** could still collapse.
I cannot assume **dispute advice** will keep paying my rent.
do: Build a **three-month fund** before buying a course.
Take **disputed accounts** and teach juniors the checking method.
Apply for **compliance posts** if paid hours fall below four days weekly.
feel: He feels **anxious**, though five years gives him time to act.
S3.quote: I don't know whether advice on messy tax disputes will stay valuable, so I won't bet my rent on it.
fieldNote: He connects a **three-month target** to a decision to delay course spending.
His move to compliance has an **hours threshold** and requires a written salary offer.

steps.text: Build savings to three months of expenses before course fees
Take disputed accounts and teach juniors his checking method
Apply for compliance posts if hours fall below four days weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should be used, not wished away. Bell & North could build a better service for the clients whose books are tangled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I'd still need work, so AGI reaching the tax desk would be serious. But ten earning years could clear my small debts and let me choose a different paid role before the fee for routine returns goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners next spring to let me run a small advisory list for tradespeople with messy accounts. Over the decade I'd save for six months of bills and take a paid compliance qualification only if employers say they require it; after 2036 I'd take the better salaried option if our tax work shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy rather than sleepless about this one. Ten years gives a careful person time to test a path without gambling the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would tell you if that advisory list is actually useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three tradespeople already ask me to explain tax letters, so I'd ask what they would pay for a quarterly visit. I wouldn't use client names without the partners' permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do robots in 2039 enter your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They matter to some of my trades clients, but the thinking side of my accounts job changes in 2036. I wouldn't postpone the savings plan to 2039.

say: I would use the **decade** to test a paid advisory service for tradespeople.
I would make Bell & North **earn trust** on tangled accounts.
think: My tax desk remains exposed in **2036**, when I would be 37.
Ten earning years could give me a **six-month cushion** and another salaried option.
do: Test a **quarterly advisory** offer with three trades clients next spring.
Save **six months** of bills before AGI reaches the desk.
Take a **paid compliance qualification** only if employers require it.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, but can test another path before tax fees shrink.
S4.quote: Ten years gives a careful person time to test a path without gambling the rent.
fieldNote: He treats **2036** as the desk-work deadline and refuses to borrow time from the later robot date.
His training choice depends on **employer demand**, while his advisory idea has three possible paying clients.

steps.text: Test quarterly advisory visits with three trades clients next spring
Save six months of bills over the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the tax desk could lose its fee before I have even a month's rent saved. A written staffing plan and a paid chance to learn dispute review would help more than a speech about change. My father could offer a spare room, but I don't want that to be my career plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs a return when a machine gets it wrong. The shop owner won't sue a screen; the responsibility lands on a person, and somebody needs to pay that person to do the checking.

headlineQuote: The shop owner won't sue a screen; the responsibility lands on a person, and somebody needs to pay that person to do the checking.
portrait: Rafael, 27, leads a **three-person team** at Bell & North and holds a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
His **senior pay** is low, and he has three weeks of expenses saved where few accounting jobs are nearby.
He uses AI **occasionally**, after others test it, and wants named human responsibility for every return.
He fears **2028 AGI** most; longer timelines let him save, test advisory work and seek paid compliance work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could strip the tax desk of fees before he saves even one month of rent.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan** and paid training in dispute review would give him a practical path.
